newsitem.title: JAPAN: Rivalry grows among Japan digital camera makers.
newsitem.headline: Rivalry grows among Japan digital camera makers.

text.p: Competition is intensifying among Japanese digital camera makers as companies try to lure more consumers to the fledgling market with an array of compact, user-friendly products, analysts say.

Manufacturers anticipate a mass future market for digital cameras, which do not need film, feature instant picture review, and can used to send pictures over the Internet. However the images are still poorer in quality than those produced by conventional cameras.

Major camera maker Olympus Optical Co Ltd, consumer electronics giants Toshiba Corp, Sony Corp and Casio Computer Co Ltd, and information equipment maker Ricoh Co Ltd are among the firms due to introduce digital cameras this summer.
While consumer electronics and information equipment makers have placed priority on ease of use and lower prices, traditional camera makers have focused more on image quality.

Japan's digital camera market tripled to 600,000 units in 1996 compared to the year before, while the overseas market reached 400,000 units from zero in the same period, said Noboru Machida, an analyst at Nikko Research Center Ltd.
He said both markets would grow two-fold this year.
Despite forecasts of buoyant growth in market size, analysts warned of heated competition and thin profit margins.
"Demand for digital cameras will grow, but profitability will be low due to fierce competition," said Masashi Ichikawa, an analyst at Wako Research Institute of Economics Inc.

In June, Toshiba unveiled the Allegretto PDR-2, which it says is the world's smallest and lightest digital camera. The business-card-sized camera, which weighs only 130 grams, can be directly inserted into computers to edit pictures.

Shortly after Toshiba's announcement, Olympus said it would launch a 260-gram Camedia C-820L in late July, featuring a 810,000-pixel charged-coupled device (CCD). It says it will be the smallest and lightest product to offer such high quality images.
So far, demand for digital cameras has mainly been from heavy users of personal computers.
But Casio and Sony said their new models were targetted at consumers who are not necessarily as computer savvy.

Casio, which enjoyed a 50 percent share in 1996, has unveiled the QV-200, a model which does not need to be linked to a computer to edit and process images. The camera itself has functions which enable the user to choose illustrations, colours and other special effects.
Sony's new Digital Mavica series uses an inexpensive and easily available 3.5-inch floppy disc as its memory device.
Users can insert the disc into a computer to process images, instead of downloading them through a cable.
"These gadgets have to be simple and handy in order to be accepted by a wide range of consumers," a Sony spokesman said.

Ricoh said last month it would launch a camera which would target a wide range of users. Its DC-2S, is the first digital camera which can send pictures via Japan's increasingly popular personal handyphone system (PHS) as well by standard phone lines to a computer or another digital camera.
So far, consumer electronic makers, with their comparatively lower prices, have taken the lead in the market over camera makers.

Analysts say they have been able to keep prices down as they themselves produce CCDs, the core of digital cameras, and because of their strategy of using CCDs with fewer pixels -- the dots that make up an electronic picture.
Camera makers have been using CCDs with more pixels in order to offer higher quality images. But this pushes up the price of the product.
Casio, the pioneer of digital cameras for consumer-use, has the biggest market share at present, analysts said.
But Tokyo camera retailer Yodobashi Camera said there were no mainstream products dominating the market yet due to the short product cycle.
